unit.title: Rate of Reaction
unit.blurb: Physical and chemical changes, conservation of mass and energy, measuring rate of reaction, collision theory, and how temperature, concentration and surface area change the rate.

O1.t: Explain why mass and energy are conserved in chemical reactions.

O2.t: Describe ways to measure rate of reaction and interpret rate graphs.

O3.t: Explain reactions using collision theory and activation energy.

O4.t: Explain how temperature, concentration and surface area affect the rate of reaction, and identify anomalous results.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 8: Rate of Reaction.
Fireworks explode in a dazzling flash,
while rust takes years to form on an old bike.
Both are chemical reactions, but at very different speeds.
What controls how fast a reaction happens?
In a physical change, like melting ice or dissolving sugar,
no new substance forms and the change can be reversed.
In a chemical change, like burning, rusting or frying an egg,
atoms rearrange to make new substances.
In a reaction, atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed:
four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms before, and the same after.
So mass is conserved.
Burnt wood only seems lighter because gases escape.
Energy is conserved too: it's transferred, not created or destroyed.
Burning charcoal transfers chemical energy to heat and light,
and photosynthesis stores the Sun's energy in glucose.

captions: The rate of reaction is how fast or slowly a reaction happens.
Fireworks and airbags react in a split second;
an airbag inflates in 30 milliseconds!
Rusting and food decaying are slow.
Some medicines must act fast, others slowly.
To measure the rate,
collect the gas made in a gas syringe at regular times,
or measure the mass lost as gas escapes.
On the graph, the steepest part is the fastest; when it's flat,
the reaction has stopped.
Marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid,
and the carbon dioxide is collected in a gas syringe.
The volume is read every 30 seconds.
In the first 30 seconds, 24 cubic centimetres of gas are collected.
In the next 30 seconds, only 16 more.
The curve gets less and less steep,
and after 150 seconds it is flat at 58 cubic centimetres.
Pause and decide: what was the average rate in the first 30 seconds,
and why does the curve level off?
Reactions happen when particles collide.
But only effective collisions make products:
the particles must meet the right way round, like puzzle pieces,
and with enough energy to break bonds.
This minimum energy is the activation energy.
Mix vinegar and baking soda and it fizzes fast at first,
because there are many particles colliding.
As they're used up, there are fewer collisions, so the reaction slows,
and stops when a reactant runs out.

captions: Two identical fizzy vitamin tablets are dropped into glasses of water at 20 degrees Celsius.
One is whole; the other has been crushed into powder.
Predict: which will stop fizzing first?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The crushed tablet fizzes much more strongly than the whole one.
The crushed tablet stops fizzing after 24 seconds.
The whole tablet takes 62 seconds.
Explain what you saw.
Crushing the tablet gives it a much larger surface area,
so many more particles are exposed to the water.
There are more collisions every second, so the reaction is faster.
Both tablets make the same amount of gas in the end,
because they have the same mass.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Raise the temperature, and particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.
They collide more often and harder, so there are more effective collisions.
An effervescent tablet fizzes much faster in hot water than in cold.
Increase the concentration, and there are more reactant particles in the same volume,
like a crowded room where people bump into each other more.
More collisions means a faster reaction.
Increase the surface area by breaking a lump into small pieces,
and more particles are exposed to collide.
Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster than marble chips,
though both make the same total amount of gas.
Line A is steeper at the start and levels off sooner,
so its reaction is faster, as with hot water or powder.
Both lines end at the same height,
because the same reactants give the same amount of product.
When you plot results,
look for any anomalous result that doesn't fit the pattern.
It might be a measuring error, so repeat that measurement to check.
The class repeats the experiment with whole tablets,
changing only the temperature of the water.
At 10 degrees Celsius the fizzing lasts 95 seconds.
At 20 degrees it lasts 62, at 40 degrees 32,
and at 60 degrees only 18.
Pause and decide: what is the pattern,
and how does collision theory explain it?
